content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the truth' is understood primarily as God's self-revelation made known and embodied in Jesus Christ — not merely accurate information but the divine reality, faithfulness, and saving revelation of God, personified in Christ and communicated through his word and gospel. The most widely repeated formulation is that Jesus does not simply teach the truth but IS the truth, so that knowing the truth means knowing him and being rightly related to God, with liberating and sanctifying effect.","primary_basis":["John 14:6 — 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life'","John 8:31–32 — 'you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free'","John 1:14, 1:17 — the Word made flesh, 'full of grace and truth'; 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ'","John 17:17 — 'Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth'","John 18:37–38 — Jesus came 'to bear witness to the truth'; Pilate's 'What is truth?'","John 4:23–24 — worship 'in spirit and truth'","John 14:17; 15:26; 16:13 — the Holy Spirit as 'the Spirit of truth' who guides into all truth","Ephesians 4:21 — 'the truth is in Jesus'","2 Thessalonians 2:10–13 — being saved through 'love of the truth' and 'belief in the truth'"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The truth as Scripture / the Word of God itself — God's written word regarded as truth and the standard of truth (a reading especially emphasized in Protestant and evangelical teaching).","basis":["John 17:17 — 'your word is truth'","Psalm 119:160 — 'the sum of your word is truth'","2 Timothy 2:15 — 'rightly handling the word of truth'"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The truth as the gospel message and the body of apostolic doctrine — 'the truth' as shorthand for orthodox Christian faith, contrasted with heresy and deception (frequent in the Pastoral Epistles and Johannine letters).","basis":["1 Timothy 2:4 — God desires all 'to come to the knowledge of the truth'","1 Timothy 3:15 — the church as 'pillar and buttress of the truth'","Galatians 2:5, 2:14 — 'the truth of the gospel'","2 John 1–4; 3 John 3–4 — 'walking in the truth'","Colossians 1:5 — 'the word of the truth, the gospel'"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The truth as the Holy Spirit's presence and work — the Spirit as 'the Spirit of truth' who reveals, testifies, and guides believers into truth; some traditions foreground this pneumatological reading.","basis":["John 14:17; 15:26; 16:13","1 John 5:6 — 'the Spirit is the truth'"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The truth as God's covenant faithfulness and reliability (Hebrew emet/emunah) — an Old Testament–grounded reading in which 'truth' means steadfastness and trustworthiness rather than propositional accuracy; prominent in academic biblical scholarship.","basis":["Exodus 34:6 — 'abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (emet)'","Psalm 25:5; Psalm 86:11 — walking in God's truth","Psalm 100:5 — 'his faithfulness endures to all generations'"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Truth as a moral and ethical virtue — honesty, integrity, and sincerity in the believer's conduct, opposed to lying and hypocrisy.","basis":["Ephesians 4:25 — 'speak the truth' with one's neighbor","Ephesians 6:14 — the 'belt of truth'","Zechariah 8:16; Proverbs 12:22","1 John 1:6, 3:18 — practicing / loving 'in deed and in truth'"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Truth as ultimate philosophical or metaphysical reality — a Greek-influenced reading (aletheia as 'unveiled reality') developed in some patristic and academic treatments, where 'the truth' is the eternal divine reality behind appearances.","basis":["John 4:24 read philosophically","Patristic and Platonic-influenced exegesis (e.g., Augustine, Origen) rather than a single proof text"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a recognizable, broadly settled consensus, but it is deliberately multi-layered: most Christian traditions treat 'the truth' as one integrated reality with several referents — Christ personally (dominant center, from John 14:6), Scripture/God's word, the gospel and apostolic doctrine, and the Spirit of truth — rather than as competing definitions. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant teaching all converge on the Christocentric core while weighting the secondary layers differently (Protestants stress Scripture as truth; Catholics/Orthodox stress the church and tradition as guardians of the truth, per 1 Tim 3:15; scholars stress the Hebrew emet sense of faithfulness). Consensus is strongest for the claim 'the truth = God's revelation in Christ' and weaker on how exclusively any single layer defines it."}
